                                                B.     Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Personal Jurisdiction
                                   1

                                   2            Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2), defendants may move to dismiss for lack

                                   3   of personal jurisdiction. While the plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the court has personal

                                   4   jurisdiction over the defendant, the court “resolves all disputed facts in favor of the plaintiff.” See
                                   5
                                       Pebble Beach Co.v. Caddy, 453 F.3d 1151, 1154 (9th Cir. 2006) (citation modified). The court
                                   6
                                       may consider evidence presented in affidavits and declarations in determining personal
                                   7
                                       jurisdiction. Data Disc, Inc. v. Sys. Tech. Assocs., Inc., 557 F.2d 1280, 1285 (9th Cir. 1977). But
                                   8
                                       when a district court acts on a 12(b)(2) motion without holding an evidentiary hearing, the
                                   9

                                  10   plaintiff need only make a prima facie showing of jurisdictional facts to withstand the motion to

                                  11   dismiss. Ballard v. Savage, 65 F.3d 1495, 1498 (9th Cir. 1995). “The plaintiff cannot simply rest
                                  12   on the bare allegations of its complaint, but uncontroverted allegations in the complaint must be

                                  16

                                  17   2014).
